title: Can two by one tiles cover a four by six grid?
description: A grid of four rows and six columns, and a tile that covers two squares. Each column holds four squares, so two upright tiles fill it, and six columns need twelve tiles. Keeko's doubt, one tile for each square, is struck.
teaching_notes: One idea: a tile covers two squares, so the number of tiles is half the number of squares, and one column at a time can be filled. Watch for students who count one tile for each square.

source: Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles? Show one way.
video_script.why: The child sees how to cover a grid, one column at a time, with tiles that each cover two squares.
video_script.substitution: Each tile covers two squares, so the count of tiles is half the count of squares.
video_script.anchor: A grid of unit squares with 4 rows and 6 columns, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko counts one tile for each square, so twenty four tiles. But each tile covers two squares, so twenty four squares need only twelve tiles.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the grid can be tiled with twelve vertical tiles, two in each column.

final_answer.value: Yes: 12 vertical tiles, 2 in each column
final_answer.spoken: yes, twelve vertical tiles, two in each column

maths_rules: The grid has 4 × 6 = 24 unit squares, and each tile covers 2, so 24 ÷ 2 = 12 tiles are needed.
Each column has 4 squares, one above another.
Two vertical tiles cover one column exactly.
Do this for all 6 columns: 6 × 2 = 12 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
Slip: one tile for each square would be 24 tiles, but a tile covers 2 squares.
video_script.design: One grid, one tile. The tile is shown upright and lying, then two upright tiles fill one column. The columns are filled in turn. The slip is one tile for each square.
